title: Family-Run Indian Restaurant Near Newark Wins National Best Restaurant Award
excerpt: The Ashiana in North Muskham takes home Best Restaurant of the Year at the Curry Life Awards, adding to a growing list of East Midlands honours.
body:
• The Ashiana Indian and Bangladeshi Restaurant in North Muskham, near Newark-on-Trent, won Best Restaurant of the Year at the national Curry Life Awards 2025 in London.
  • Founded in 2008 by Saiqul Miah, the family-run restaurant is housed in a former country pub on the A1 and serves freshly cooked Bangladeshi and Indian cuisine tailored to each customer.
  • The restaurant previously won Restaurant of the Year – East Midlands at the Asian Restaurant and Takeaway Awards (ARTA) and Best Bangladeshi Restaurant at the English Curry Awards 2023.
  • With a 4.9-star rating and loyal customers who drive up to 90 minutes for a meal, the Ashiana has become one of the most decorated Indian restaurants in the East Midlands.

A family-run Indian and Bangladeshi restaurant tucked away on the A1 near Newark-on-Trent has cemented its reputation as one of Britain's finest, taking home the Best Restaurant of the Year title at the national Curry Life Awards 2025.

The Ashiana Indian and Bangladeshi Restaurant, located in the village of North Muskham in Nottinghamshire, beat competition from across the country at a ceremony hosted by ITV broadcaster Nina Hossain at the Marriott Grosvenor Square in Mayfair, London, the Newark and Sherwood News Journal reported.

From Country Pub to Award Winner

Owner Saiqul Miah founded the Ashiana in 2008, converting a period country pub on Bathley Lane into a restaurant that has since built a devoted following. The restaurant prides itself on cooking every dish fresh to order using locally sourced ingredients, and staff regularly tailor curries to individual customer preferences.

"Our first-class service is friendly and welcoming, and we would expect you to have an unforgettable experience when you visit us."

— Saiqul Miah, Owner, Ashiana Restaurant

The menu draws on both Indian and Bangladeshi culinary traditions, with signature dishes including duck bahari — tandoori stone quail lightly spiced with winter herbs, curry leaves and button onions — along with badami lamb and king prawn pakoras. The restaurant also offers alfresco dining in a dedicated garden and operates a separate takeaway at nearby Long Bennington.

A Growing Collection of Honours

The Curry Life Award is the latest in a string of national and regional recognitions. In 2022, the Ashiana was crowned Restaurant of the Year – East Midlands at the Asian Restaurant and Takeaway Awards (ARTA), described as the largest celebration of Britain's Asian restaurant and takeaway industry. That ceremony was held at the InterContinental Hotel at The O2 in London, hosted by BBC journalist Samantha Simmonds.

The restaurant also won Best Bangladeshi Restaurant at the English Curry Awards 2023, selected from over 7,000 national entries. Combined with a 4.9-star average rating from customer reviews, the Ashiana has built a reputation that extends well beyond Nottinghamshire — reviewers on TripAdvisor frequently note driving over an hour to eat there.

The Bangladeshi Restaurant Scene in Britain

The Ashiana's success reflects the enduring strength of Bangladeshi-run restaurants in Britain's curry industry. Bangladeshi families have been the backbone of the UK's Indian restaurant sector since the 1960s, operating the majority of the country's estimated 12,000 curry houses. Despite challenges including rising costs, staff shortages and competition from delivery apps, family-run establishments like the Ashiana continue to thrive by emphasising quality ingredients and personalised service.

The restaurant employs a small team and is open 364 days a year. Miah has described the hospitality industry as playing "a crucial role in the economy, providing jobs and a place for people to celebrate special occasions."

What Makes It Stand Out

Diners consistently praise the Ashiana for three things: the quality and freshness of the food, the warmth of the service and the willingness to cook off-menu. One TripAdvisor reviewer who has visited for years noted: "What's unique about this place is they can make you literally anything. They do all the sauces separately so you can order a chicken tikka shashlik with modu sauce or masala."

For diaspora food lovers in the UK, the Ashiana represents a model of what a family-run South Asian restaurant can achieve — national recognition built not on trendy reinvention but on consistency, hospitality and respect for traditional flavours.
